articles.title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
articles.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of a conference.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China has been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East By Koh Ewe 
- Published 16 October 2026 
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said. 
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday. 
Beijing has been a long-standing supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction". 
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East. 
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran . 
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity. 
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented. 
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe". 
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", he said. 
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East". 
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote. 
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme. 
China itself has been accused of trying to dilute its minority populations by encouraging Han Chinese migration to Tibet, which it annexed in the 1950s, and Xinjiang. Beijing rejects those claims, saying its policies promote economic development and social stability. 
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges. 
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day . More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. 
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. 
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

articles.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
articles.summary: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea By Koh Ewe   and   Julianna Khan 
- Published 15 October 2026 
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours. 
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme. 
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them. 
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty. 
Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties. 
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region. 
The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges". 
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea. 
A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC. 
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds. 
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually." 
Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Why did Xi Jinping visit North Korea? 
But the alliance is not without tension. 
Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan. 
China's attitude has shifted more recently. 
"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC. 
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war. 
At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops. 
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day. 
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties. 
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. 
"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. 
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children' By Stephen McDonell 
China correspondent 
- Published 13 October 2026 
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV." 
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia. 
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer." 
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner. 
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact". 
There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country. 
Image caption, 
Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own. 
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives. 
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that. 
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs. 
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine." 
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added. 
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver. 
Image caption, 
Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents. 
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible. 
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows. 
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles. 
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile. 
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC. 
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult. 
Image caption, 
Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit. 
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood. 
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him. 
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits. 
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic. 
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards." 
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves. 
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious." 
Image caption, 
Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals. 
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection. 
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee. 
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect." 
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province. 
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said. 
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month. 
Image caption, 
Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan. 
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said. 
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her." 
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude. 
"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback." 
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity. 
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly. 
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said. 
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy. 
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
articles.summary: With the festive season on the horizon, we trace toys from factories in China to US shelves.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US By Sam Fenwick Host – Follow the Money: Business Daily 
- Published 15 October 2026 
On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China". 
Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external 
Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external 
With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far. 
As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes. 
The factory 
Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry. 
In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting. 
The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business. 
- 
Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America 
Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed. 
Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it." 
Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months. 
Image source, Mihox Image caption, 
The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people 
So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang. 
On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes. 
Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it. 
Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour. 
He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive." 
And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises. 
Image source, Mihox Image caption, 
Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price 
Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year. 
Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so. 
The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories. 
Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries. 
The ship 
From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong. 
Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance. 
Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September. 
Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents. 
The US border 
Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). 
Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more. 
This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents. 
This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China. 
"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg. 
The US toy company 
Image source, Basic Fun Image caption, 
Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the country 
The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total. 
That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys. 
"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says. 
If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each. 
While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50. 
Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.

articles.title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
articles.summary: Can Nepal bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in the Himalayas?
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The recent floods in Nepal have highlighted the need for cross-border co-operation in the Himalayan region By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 15 October 2026 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. 
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. 
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. 
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. 
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. 
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. 
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. 
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? 
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. 
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. 
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. 
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Balendra Shah has urged neighbours India and China to collaborate on climate risks in the Himalayan region 
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development , external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. 
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. 
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. 
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. 
And the dangers extend beyond flooding. 
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. 
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. 
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. 
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. 
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. 
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. 
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hundreds of people were killed in the deadly flood that tore through the China-Nepal border in August 
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. 
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. 
"What happened after that no one knows," he added. 
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. 
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. 
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. 
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes. 
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group. 
But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved. 
One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value. 
"What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Experts have raised concerns over climate-related risks as the Himalayan snow cover melts rapidly 
Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders. 
The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow. 
"There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD. 
He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks. 
Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay. 
"Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says. 
Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. 
For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat.

articles.title: Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
articles.summary: Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Trump: New White House press secretary should 'reconsider' job By Brandon Drenon Reporting from Washington DC 
- Published 3 hours ago 
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax. 
Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider". 
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters. 
She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job. 
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One. 
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said. 
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media. 
The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later. 
As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House. 
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X. 
Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president. 
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam. 
She replied: "When I was in China." 
After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam. 
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials". 
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday. 
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'" 
Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?" 
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning. 
She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one. 
Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?" 
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me." 
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team. 
In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days. 
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

articles.title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
articles.summary: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Azerbaijani social media Image caption, 
These schoolgirls were not allowed to enter classes because of their headscarves By Rayhan Demytrie Caucasus correspondent 
- Published 15 October 2026 
"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school. 
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?" 
Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad. 
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people. 
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that. 
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail. 
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally. 
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni. 
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order". 
Image source, Social media Image caption, 
Videos have circulated of protests taking place in and around the capital Baku 
The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October. 
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education." 
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday. 
In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison." 
Image source, Azerbaijan education ministry Image caption, 
An example shared by the Azerbaijani government of an acceptable school uniform under the new rules 
Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class. 
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since. 
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed. 
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN). 
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran. 
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself. 
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites. 
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility. 
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families. 
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.

- Published 23 September 
- 
Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump 
- Published 9 August 2025 
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh. 
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states". 
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation". 
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake". 
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X. 
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in. 
Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der. 
President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs. 
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life". 
Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil. 
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries. 
That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

articles.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
articles.summary: Australia has proposed a switch to force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work By Tiffanie Turnbull Sydney 
- Published 5 hours ago 
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder 
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old. 
Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition. 
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day. 
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC. 
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't." 
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words. 
Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBC Image caption, 
Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder 
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week. 
The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow. 
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality. 
Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier. 
But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech. 
The choice 
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral. 
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago. 
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric. 
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order. 
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC. 
"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character." 
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay. 
Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC News Image caption, 
Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media 
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man." 
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor. 
Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users. 
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools. 
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture. 
Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction , external ; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health , external , and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline . 
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line. 
"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC. 
Image source, Cordelia Hsu/Reuters Image caption, 
Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021 
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change. 
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them. 
Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite. 
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts. 
The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off. 
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said. 
"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them." 
- 
Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears 
- Published 18 August 
- 
Social media is 'deliberately' addictive 
- Published 4 July 2018 
Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images Image caption, 
Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill 
The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment". 
Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m). 
"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC. 
The challenges 
There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation. 
In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise . 
"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney. 
Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoyment 
Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship. 
But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week. 
The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children. 
However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban ? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media ban 
The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale. 
Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that. 
"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation , external . 
On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return. 
The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act. 
Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feeds 
The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app. 
Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global. 
"We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing." 
Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them. 
Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment." 
Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off. 
Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice. 
"On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good." 
If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line .

articles.full_text:
China disaster simulator in Hangzhou 
China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies 
W hen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods. 
“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China . “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.” 
She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario. 
View image in fullscreen 
Participants brace for surging water in a flash flood simulator at the Lvxing centre in Hangzhou. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters 
View image in fullscreen 
Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters 
Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.” 
Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”. 
Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments. 
At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster. 
“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.” 
It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations. 
View image in fullscreen 
People want to feel ‘what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like’, says general manager Wang Kuanghan. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters 
The offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake. 
Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country. 
In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis. 
‘A new generation of travellers’
“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. 
But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction. 
In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside. 
View image in fullscreen 
A classroom inside a destroyed school building lies preserved following the 2008 Sichuan earthquake at Beichuan. Photograph: Wu Hong/EPA 
In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck. 
“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.” 
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered. 
In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”. 
View image in fullscreen 
People choose chrysanthemums to dedicate to victims at the Nanjing Massacre memorial hall in September 2026. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images 
Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says. 
“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang. 
Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.

An electric vehicle production line in Ningbo, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters 
View image in fullscreen 
An electric vehicle production line in Ningbo, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters 
No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package 
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”. 
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme . 
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme. 
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures. 
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”. 
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy. 
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU. 
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”. 
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.” 
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share. 
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027. 
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants. 
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc. 
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway. 
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”. 
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China. 
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector. 
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation. 
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars. 
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry. 
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU. 
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”. 
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy. 
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.full_text:
The renowned Beijing-based architecture firm Turenscape came up with the museum’s bold design. Photograph: Turenscape 
How architects worked with harsh environment to create sustainable building in location where fossils were found By Xiaoying You 
V iewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China , the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen. 
Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment. 
View image in fullscreen 
The Hami Pterosaur Museum is designed so as to require minimal artificial heating and cooling. Photograph: Turenscape 
The Hami region is notorious for its scorching summers. Air temperatures can exceed 55C (131F), while the surface ground temperature can reach 80C, says Wang Xiaolin, the director of the museum and a palaeontologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Violent winds and sandstorms terrorise the area frequently, according to Xiaolin, who has carried out excavation work in Hami for 20 years. 
Despite the intimidating conditions, building the museum in the area is important from a scientific perspective because this is where the fossils were buried and found, Xiaolin says. Keeping the fossils local protects the fragile relics and lets visitors see them in their geological context, he adds. 
Visitors to the five exhibition halls can expect to see precious fossils discovered by Xiaolin’s team, including one that has preserved the upper and lower jaws, as well as the soft-tissue structures of the head crest of a pterosaur that roamed the area roughly 130m years ago. 
View image in fullscreen 
Most of the museum’s structure has been built 8-metres deep into the ground of the desert. Photograph: Turenscape 
Most of the 8,000-sq metre museum is built 8 metres into the ground where temperatures are much lower, which helps it stay cool in summer, says Huai Kaifeng, an architect at Beijing-based Turenscape, which designed the project. In winter, when temperatures can drop below -20C, the design also helps the museum stay warm. 
Being largely underground, with seven above-ground entrances, allows the museum to use its energy as efficiently as possible, says Wang Yujia, a landscape architect and associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in the US, who is not involved in the project. Most of it is able to avoid direct exposure to wind, sand and solar heat and the large temperature swings between day and night in the desert. “This all means that you need much, much less air-conditioning,” Yujia says. 
View image in fullscreen 
Visitors to the museum will be able to see the fossils in the geological context of where they were found. Photograph: Turenscape 
Although air-conditioners have been installed to provide backup, the museum has natural ventilation shafts that allow cool air to sink and hot air to rise and escape. The museum can cut its electricity usage on air conditioning by 94% compared with an above-ground counterpart, according to estimates by Turenscape. This equates to a saving of 223,421kWh of electricity annually – enough to power an average UK home for 89 years. 
But the underground space in the desert presented another challenge for the architects: lighting. The team used giant, translucent, ceiling-to-floor funnels to let in as much natural light as possible. These structures slash the museum’s need for artificial lighting by nearly 50%, saving 84,672kWh of electricity a year, according to Turenscape. 
The museum was one of the last designs completed by the late Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu , the founder of Turenscape. Yu was the brain behind China’s “ sponge cities ”, a concept that uses nature to prevent flooding in urban areas. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion ‘If you’re flushing the toilet with grey water, people should know’: how China turned rain into an asset 
Read more 
The museum has its own micro power grid, featuring a solar farm and batteries to store energy. The solar farm is about 1km from the museum, with an outline resembling that of a pterosaur when viewed from above. It is expected to generate more than 22.4GWh of electricity a year, enough to meet the museum’s own demand, Huai says. The museum is still connected to the power grid of the nearby city of Hami to ensure its energy security, he notes. 
The museum is also connected to Hami’s water-supplying network, but it has a recycling system on site to collect, process and reuse its grey water. 
“Water is precious out here in the Gobi,” Xiaolin says. 
For Yujia, the museum is a good example of how a building can be designed to adapt to its natural environment rather than fight against it. 
Although technology enables people to build luxury resorts in a desert and keep them cool, such projects require huge amounts of energy and resources, he says. 
“It makes sense to work as much as possible with the environmental conditions that are already there, instead of relying entirely on technology to isolate the building from them.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Pterosaurs once roamed the Hami region roughly 130m years ago. Photograph: Turenscape 
Examples include a floating exhibition pavilion built in Rotterdam to address rising sea levels, and a giant park with a tilted ground in Bangkok that aims to prevent urban flooding, and a home shaped like a snail’s shell in Iran to help its inhabitants stay cool. 
The concept is important for arid areas. “These places are not cities, you don’t necessarily have the basic infrastructure or the resources you desire even if you pay, because money is not magic,” Yujia adds. 
Designing buildings and parks to combat natural disasters was a lasting theme throughout Yu’s career, and for Jiinyi Hwang, the chief architect at Turenscape, the museum is no exception. 
“Our world is drying. Deserts and arid zones are expanding. Cities are warming. More and more of the built environment is being pushed into climates that were once considered unbuildable,” Hwang says. “If we keep designing with the same assumptions – sealed boxes, glass facades and mechanical climate control – we will consume the very resources these landscapes cannot spare.”

Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model
Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals 
Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers. 
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X. 
Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them. ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness 
Read more 
Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years. 
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level. 
“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model. 
Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies. 
Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said. 
The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude. 
Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.
